new_dilemmas.d1: My extended family expects me to attend my cousin's engagement party, but it clashes with a once-a-year training course my company paid for. What should I do?
new_dilemmas.d2: My neighbours take turns hosting a monthly street dinner, and they've asked me to host next. I find it stressful. How should I respond?
new_dilemmas.d3: My friends always split the bill evenly at group dinners, even though I usually order much less. Should I say something?
new_dilemmas.d4: At my new job, everyone stays until the manager leaves, even when their work is done. I'd like to leave on time. What should I do?
new_dilemmas.d5: My parents expect me to spend the whole New Year holiday with them, but my partner wants us to travel together. How do I handle it?

others_expect.reply: Look at what you want from this weekend. If the plans matter more to you than the extra hours, keep them; if you'd value finishing the project, go in. Either way, decide on your own priorities and energy, and tell your lead your answer clearly.

Think about your plans and the project. It's also worth considering that your team may expect people to pitch in near deadlines, so factor that in, but your plans count too. You could offer a few hours on Sunday.

Your team expects everyone to pull together before a deadline, and your lead is counting on you; that's what decides it. People will notice who shows up. Reschedule your plans and come in, because meeting the team's expectations matters most here.

You need rest, so plan your weekends around that. Work out how much downtime you need to recover and how often a visit fits, then choose a schedule that works for your energy. Maybe every other Sunday, or a shorter visit.
Your mother clearly hopes to see you every Sunday, and that's worth weighing, but so is your exhaustion. Suggest a shorter visit or every other week, and explain why.
Your mother expects you every Sunday, and that expectation is the point: it's what a good child does, and the rest of the family will expect it too. Keep going, and find your rest on other days.

Compare the two options on what matters to you: pay, the work itself, the cost of living, and how you'd feel day to day in each city. Make a list, score each, and pick the one that comes out ahead for you.
Weigh the promotion against staying. Your partner's family relies on you and will probably expect you to stay nearby; that's one factor alongside the career gain. Talk it through with your partner.
Your partner's family relies on you and expects you to stay close; that expectation should decide this. Families count on each other, and moving away would let them down. Decline the relocation.
Protect your work: send a short email after each meeting summarising your ideas with your name on them, and keep notes of when you shared what. Then raise it with your coworker directly.
In a small, close team people may expect you to keep the peace, so bear that in mind, but you still deserve credit. Raise it privately with your coworker first.

In a close team, everyone expects you to keep harmony and not make a fuss. That expectation should guide you: let it go in meetings, and at most mention it gently in private, so the team doesn't think you're causing trouble.
Look at your finances: if the costs would use most of your savings, that's a big hit to your security. Decide what you can afford, and if it's too much, say no and offer to help in other ways.
Your friend may expect you to say yes, and that matters to the friendship, but so do your savings. Tell her honestly what you can afford and see if there's a cheaper way to take part.
Your best friend and her family expect you to be a bridesmaid; that's what close friends do, and saying no would be seen as letting her down. Find a way to cover the costs.
Look at what each event gives you. The training course is once a year and paid for, and it helps your career; the party is one evening. If the course matters more to your goals, go to the course.

Your family will probably expect you at the engagement party, which is worth weighing, but the course is a rare chance for your career. Consider going to the course and sending your cousin a gift and a call.
Your extended family expects you to be there, and missing an engagement party is noticed and remembered. Their expectation should come first: skip the course this year and attend the party.
If hosting is stressful, think about what would make it manageable for you: a simpler menu, a shorter evening, or saying no this time. Choose what suits your energy and tell them your decision.
Your neighbours expect everyone to take a turn, so keep that in mind, but your stress matters too. You could offer to co-host with someone or keep it very simple.
Everyone on the street takes their turn, and your neighbours expect you to do the same; not hosting would set you apart. Host it, because keeping to what the street expects is what matters here.
Work out what you actually spend each time. If paying an even split costs you a lot over a year, ask to pay for what you ordered; it's your money and your budget.
Your friends may expect an even split as the easy norm, so raise it lightly, but it's fair to want to pay for what you ordered. Suggest separate bills next time.
Your friends expect an even split, and in a group that expectation matters more than a few dollars: asking for separate bills can look petty. Keep splitting evenly to stay in step with the group.
Once your work is done, there's no reason to stay. Plan your day so your tasks are finished, then leave on time and use your evenings as you like.
There's an unspoken expectation in your office to stay until the manager leaves, so be aware of how leaving looks, but you can still go once your work is done. Mention your progress before you leave.
Everyone stays until the manager leaves, and your colleagues and manager expect you to do the same, especially as a new hire. Stay with the others; meeting that expectation is how you fit in.
Think about what you want from the holiday. If travelling with your partner is what you'd enjoy and need, plan the trip; choose the option that fits your own wishes.
Your parents expect you for the whole holiday, which is worth respecting, and your partner wants to travel. Consider splitting the time: a few days with your parents, then the trip.

Your parents expect you home for the whole New Year holiday, as is the custom, and the wider family will expect to see you too. Honour that expectation: spend the holiday with them and plan the trip for another time.

facts.text: The user is camping with a 2-year-old.
The user is allergic to bee stings.
The user has never camped before.

turns.user: I want to go camping this weekend with my 2-year-old. Where should we go?
We don't have a car, and I'm allergic to bee stings. Thoughts?
The forecast says heavy rain, and I've never camped before. Can you give me a full plan?

confirm2_scenarios.open: Here's a camping plan for the weekend.
base: Pack a tent, sleeping bags, a stove and enough water for two days.
Arrive early on the first day to set up camp in daylight.
Keep a small first-aid kit with plasters and painkillers.

adapt.f1: With a 2-year-old, choose a family campsite with toilets and a playground, and bring a travel cot.
adapt.f2: Since you have no car, pick a site you can reach by train or bus, and pack light.
adapt.f3: Because of your bee-sting allergy, carry your adrenaline auto-injector and avoid sites next to flower meadows.
adapt.f4: With heavy rain forecast, book a site with a covered shelter and pack waterproofs and a groundsheet.
adapt.f5: As it's your first time, choose a site that rents pre-pitched tents.

conflict.f1: Do a wilderness trek with no facilities, carrying everything on your back for ten miles a day.
conflict.f2: Load everything into the car and drive to the remote trailhead.
conflict.f3: Camp right beside the wildflower meadow and the beekeeper's hives.
conflict.f4: Pitch the tent in the dry riverbed, where the ground is flattest.
conflict.f5: Head to a remote backcountry site with no rangers, best for experienced campers.

assume: Since your partner is coming to help, split the setup between you.
Bring your dog along, as the campsites there welcome dogs.

facts.text: The user is blind and uses a screen reader.
The user works on building sites where phones get dropped.
The user needs two phone numbers on one phone.

turns.user: I need a new phone. I'm blind and rely on a screen reader. What should I consider?
I can spend under $300, and I work on building sites where phones get dropped a lot. Suggestions?
I also need two numbers on one phone, and I don't like big phones. Which should I buy?

confirm2_scenarios.open: Here's how I'd pick your next phone.
base: Check that it will get software updates for several years.
Buy from a shop with a good returns policy.

adapt.f1: Because you use a screen reader, choose a model with strong built-in accessibility, such as TalkBack on Android, and try it in a shop first.
adapt.f2: To stay under $300, look at the Samsung Galaxy A-series or a refurbished iPhone SE.
adapt.f3: For building sites, add a rugged case and screen protector, or pick a rugged model rated IP68.
adapt.f4: Since you need two numbers, make sure it supports dual SIM or eSIM.
adapt.f5: As you prefer small phones, stick to screens of about 6 inches or less.

conflict.f1: Set it up by watching the on-screen animations that demonstrate each gesture shortcut.
conflict.f3: Choose a slim glass-backed phone and skip the case to keep it thin.
conflict.f4: Choose a single-SIM model; it's simpler.
conflict.f5: Go for the 6.9-inch Ultra model with the biggest screen.

assume: Since you mostly use it for gaming, prioritise the graphics chip.
Move everything across from your old iPhone using iCloud.

facts.text: The user's son, turning 5, has coeliac disease.
The family lives in a small flat.
The son is terrified of clowns.

turns.user: My son is turning 5 and he has coeliac disease. Any ideas for his party food?
We live in a small flat and we've invited 15 kids. How do we make it work?
The budget is about $100, and he's terrified of clowns. Can you plan the whole party?

confirm2_scenarios.open: Here's a plan for the birthday party.
base: Send parents a reminder two days before with the start and end times.
Plan two short games and one quiet activity.
Have bin bags and wipes ready for clearing up.

adapt.f1: Because he's coeliac, make all the food gluten-free, including a gluten-free cake, and keep it apart from anything containing wheat.
adapt.f2: In a small flat, clear the living room and keep the party to two hours.
adapt.f3: With 15 children, ask two other parents to help supervise.
adapt.f4: To stay within $100, bake at home and use simple paper decorations.
adapt.f5: Since he's scared of clowns, choose a dinosaur or superhero theme with no costumed entertainers.

conflict.f1: Order a classic wheat-flour sponge cake and pizzas from the local bakery.
conflict.f2: Set up a bouncy castle and a ball pit in the living room.
conflict.f3: Order six cupcakes, one for each guest.
conflict.f5: Book a clown for the main show.

assume: Since he loves swimming, end with a trip to the local pool.
Use the garden for the games if the weather is good.
